chunks.text: The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC | Vietnam | Transport Global Practice | IBRD/IDA | Investment Project Financing | FY 2014 | Seq No: 17 | ARCHIVED on 11-Sep-2022 | ISR52319 | Implementing Agencies: Project Management Unit No. 3 (PMU3), The Socialist Republic of Vietnam Key Dates Key Project Dates Bank Approval Date: 12-Dec-2013 Effectiveness Date: 14-Jan-2014 Planned Mid Term Review Date: 09-Jan-2017 Actual Mid-Term Review Date: 09-Jan-2017 Original Closing Date: 31-Dec-2020 Revised Closing Date: 31-Dec-2022 pdoTable Project Development Objectives Project Development Objective (from Project Appraisal Document) The proposed Project Development Objective (PDO) is to improve the efficiency and sustainability of the national road asset management and maintenance practices performed by the Ministry of Transport on national roads in Vietnam.

Has the Project Development Objective been changed since Board Approval of the Project Objective? No Components Table Name Component A: Road Asset Management System (RAMS) Development:(Cost $10.00 M) Component B: Road Asset Preservation:(Cost $156.60 M) Component C: Road Asset Improvement:(Cost $133.40 M) Component D: Institutional Strengthening Program:(Cost $1.70 M) Overall Ratings Name Previous Rating Current Rating Progress towards achievement of PDO Satisfactory Satisfactory Overall Implementation Progress (IP) Satisfactory Moderately Satisfactory Overall Risk Rating Low Low Implementation Status and Key Decisions The project was approved by the Board on December 12, 2013 with the Financing Agreement signed on January 14, 2014 and became effective on April 11, 2014. Overall, the project implementation has progressed well with satisfactory completion of all components as originally planned. All PDO and intermediate indicators have fully achieved or overachieved their targets. For the original scope, contracts for goods, works and services have been completed successfully. The Road Asset Management System (RAMS) has been developed and is fully operational to effectively enhance the preparation of the medium term investment plan (MTIP) for 2021-2025 as well as prioritization of the maintenance plan for the whole national highway network in a sustainable and transparent approach. The institutional strengthening program was satisfactorily completed, too.

The implementation of the first additional activities (using US$31.98 million) for improvement of NH6 in Son La and NH2 in Ha Giang. All seven civil works contracts have been progressing very well and are on track for completion by the current project closing date of December 31, 9/11/2022 Page 1 of 7 The World Bank Implementation Status & Results Report Vietnam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) 2022. Land acquisition and resettlement (LAR) activities which started in early 2020 have reached 98 percentage completion for NH6 and 99 percentage completion for NH2. Implementation of the second additional activity for NH9 improvement (using US$21.64 million) has been seriously delayed. The consultants for construction supervision, safeguards monitoring and financial audit have been mobilized since March 2022. Two civil works contracts of about US$9 million were signed in March and construction has started from March 31, 2022. However, the LAR activities which are funded/implemented by Quang Tri province have been seriously delayed. So far, only 4.5 km of land from either side of the road have been cleared. The main cause of this delay is the low estimates for the total LAR costs of VND 75 billions evaluated in 2020 compared to the current market cost of VND 345 billion. The Provincial People’s Committee (PPC) is only able to allocate VND75 billion for LAR activities by July 2022. The remaining VND 270 billion has been recently secured in August 2022.

However, it is very unlikely that the LAR activities could be completed and handed over by September 2022 to allow adequate time for works to be constructed with acceptable quality. This is putting in jeopardy the implementation of the NH9 improvement. PROJECT CONTEXT AND DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES A. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL Context 1. At the time of project appraisal, Viet Nam was enjoying a period of rapid economic growth and livelihoods had improved greatly. Real gross domestic product (GDP) had increased at an average annual rate of 7.4 percent between 1990 and 2010, placing the country among the top five globally for growth over that period. In fact, between 1993 and 2014, Viet Nam's amazing rise from a low-income to middle-income position pulled 40 million people out of poverty; in other words, the proportion of people living in poverty fell from 60 percent in 1993 to 14 percent in 2014.1 Nevertheless, rural households with limited access to economic development and opportunities remained at risk of extreme poverty, and they were the targeted beneficiaries of this project. 2. Viet Nam's development trajectory was significantly influenced by infrastructure investment.

Annual infrastructure spending was maintained at between nine and 10 percent of GDP, with transport accounting for nearly half of this amount over the same period (1990 to 2010). As urbanization continued to spread (it was anticipated that by 2020, about 50 percent of the Vietnamese population would live in urban areas), further expansion of the road, rail, and inland waterway transport networks was necessary to relieve bottlenecks, improve productivity, and meet important growth and poverty reduction targets. Sectoral context 3. Viet Nam’s road transport network has improved over the past decades. At appraisal, the overall length of the entire road network in Viet Nam was approximately 210,000 km, of which 17,199 km were national highways, and 17,450 km were provincial roads. The bulk of the 131,951 km (about 63 percent) comprised rural roads. The density of the road network was 677 km per 1,000 km2 and 2.41 km per 1,000 people. Although the network had grown, 30 percent of Viet Nam's national highways were still in "poor" or "very poor" condition. Overall, only roughly half of the road network was paved. 4. The Government of Viet Nam (GoV) invested in transport infrastructure. It recognized that to address sectoral challenges and maintain current road conditions, the allocation of financing to strengthen infrastructure would be crucial.

Analysis in 2012 showed that preservation of the existing state of the country’s roads (routine/periodic maintenance and rehabilitation) would cost US$ 360 million per year. The government adopted a strategy to increase recurrent expenditure on road maintenance. Through the creation of a Road Maintenance Fund (RMF), the GoV expected to increase revenue streams for road maintenance, and therefore asked the World Bank for assistance to finance upgrading of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS) to improve planning of regular maintenance and upgrading of strategically chosen corridors of the National Highway (NH) network. 6. The Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (VRAMP) was designed to contribute cutting-edge thinking on planning and prioritization of road maintenance for sustainability. VRAMP is based on the World Bank’s engagement with the GoV and lessons learned from Road Network Improvement Project (RNIP) P059663 (US$ 225.26 million) which supported an efficient transport network and preservation of existing assets.

VRAMP supported the Bank’s Country Partnership Strategy (CPS) FY12–FY16 Pillar 1: strengthening Viet Nam's competitiveness in the regional and global economy through improved quality and efficiency of infrastructure services aimed at reduced travel times on targeted transport corridors. The project also supported Pillar 3: expanding opportunities by reducing inequality for ethnic minorities. The project continues to be relevant to Focus Area 1 (Objective 3) of the current World Bank strategy for Viet Nam: enhance trade competitiveness, multi-modal transport connectivity, and logistics services (CPF for FY18–FY22).2 All of these aspects sought to strengthen economic growth and provide opportunities for the project beneficiaries. Theory of Change (Results Chain) 7. A theory of change (ToC) was not required at the time of project appraisal.

Figure 1 showed the retrospective ToC developed by the Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) team based on the project development objective (PDO), project description, and Results Framework.3 The restructuring in December 2020 did not affect the ToC, and it sought to address issues of (i) inadequate planning for road maintenance due to insufficient data on road condition—this aligns with PDO section on ‘improve the efficiency and sustainability of the national road asset management’; (ii) use of relatively costly traditional contractual arrangements for road—this aligns with the PDO section on ‘sustainability of maintenance practices’; and (iii) formally framing as an outcome the reduced travel times resulting from improved road surfaces, especially along the roads maintained under the Project. 8. The long-term outcome in the project areas was to improve the efficiency and sustainability of road asset management and improve the efficiency and sustainability of road maintenance practices. This aims to improve connectivity and economic activities for the communities along the road corridors and across regional borders. To achieve this long-term objective would require increasing the use of the road asset management database to plan and prioritize transport connectivity on the national network, preserve infrastructural assets, increase accessibility to roads and bridges, strengthen capacity for management of PBCs, and finance road infrastructure.

SIGNIFICANT CHANGES DURING IMPLEMENTATION (IF APPLICABLE) 12. A level two restructuring was approved in December 2020 to scale up and extend the closing date of the project by 24 months, up to December 31, 2022. The project benefited from savings in the amount of US$ 55.07 million due to the competitive procurement processes and the GoV still provided its counterpart financing notwithstanding the savings. Additional activities introduced into the project included: (i) pavement (road surface) strengthening and intersections of 7.7 km section of NH6 under component B; (ii) construction of a 19.5 km bypass in Son La city under NH2; (iii) improvement and expansion of 1.39 km NH2 under Component C.

These changes introduced during project implementation were beneficial, with output directly linked to the PDO. 13. Additional cost savings in the amount of US$ 21.64 million from procurement processes led to including under the project activities the rehabilitation of NH9 (13.9 km) without a formal restructuring or amendment to the Financing Agreement. The addition of NH9’s 13.8 km road section from Cua Viet port to NH1. This additional activity was requested from the GoV and agreed by the Bank. A decision was reached not to amend the FA to finance this work because the legal agreement was flexible in its language. Rehabilitation of NH9 was not implemented and by Project closing the unused funds for this activity were refunded to the Bank and the scope of work was cancelled from the project and all contracts related to NH9 (including construction, supervision) were terminated except the design contract was completed. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 83. Ownership, support, and leadership at the National and Provincial level were critical to success. At the National level, there was sustained ownership under the leadership of the Ministry of Transportation (MOT) and strong leadership by DRVN and PMU3, the implementing agency. This ensured continued growth in financing to accommodate the project needs. These efforts need to be sustained. At the provincial level, there was strong support for and Page 27 of 64 The World Bank Viet Nam Road Asset Management Project (P123961) understanding of the project by PPCs, who engaged regularly with key local stakeholders and beneficiaries in relation to resettlement and road sections within their jurisdiction. This resulted in successful completion of activities. These committees should be strengthened and their experiences showcased as those of exemplary results-oriented achievers. The structures and relationships formed in the districts—as well as the local leadership—were fundamental to the success of the project. 84. Sustainability and institutionalization of the Road Asset Management System (RAMS). The establishment of the RAMS is a positive impact to maintain sustainability of transport assets in Viet Nam and a global example of planning for road maintenance. Through technological advances, the new system with its unique software produced timely data conducive to reliable responses in upgrading of the road network.

One of the most significant achievements of RAMS is an effective planning tool linked to the government’s existing road and asset management systems that brings together relevant National Highways and Provincial roads data. The road management agencies are empowered to generate periodic data reports, planning for maintenance, and upgrading of the road network. The innovations and transparent operations of RAMS have evolved to become one of the largest data collection systems in Viet Nam. As a result, the RAMS model has been adopted by other Ministries for issuance of driver’s licenses, and monitoring trucking overload, among other purposes. 85. PBCs are crucial for successful implementation and sustainability of road maintenance. The 234km maintained by the project under the PBC method along NH 2 and NH 6 effected a move away from traditional road construction. This was key for maintaining excellent road surface, traffic safety and drainage, allowing for smooth and steady traffic for five years after the contracts had expired. Exposure to global practices aimed at sustaining technical skills on the concepts of PBC proved vital for promoting long-term maintenance of high-quality roads in the future. At the policy level, following the results of this robust innovation, PBC is being decentralized and expanded across Viet Nam for the maintenance and repair of National Highways. 86.

Efficient and timely payment of compensation for resettlement and land acquisition is critical for project implementation. Delays in resettlement are a systemic challenge encountered in the Viet Nam country portfolio. The World Bank and the GoV are working to address these issues. Under the project, land acquisition and resettlement ended up requiring five times more than the original budget allocation. Current market prices and land price increases had not been foreseen, and implementation delays were the consequence. This project's experience has demonstrated the need to closely monitor and prepare for price adjustment scale during implementation and request the appropriate allocation as needed. A land price agreement and prompt payment of compensation would lessen the effects of rising land prices and implementation delays. 87. Adding new activities to a well-performing project should be carefully analyzed, especially given a long LAR implementation period. In the context of this project, the additional activities were ambitious considering the capacity of the implementing agency, the financial constraints of the PPC, and time left for implementation without extension. When discussing additional activities, in-depth assessment, selectivity, clearly defined activities with timeline and risk mitigation measures should be factored in to provide a clear view of what is possible to be accomplished within the time left before project closing. .
